analysis.one_liner: Gives every child $1,000 at birth plus yearly federal deposits in a savings account for college, a home, or investing.
analysis.headline: The bill, which had 33 cosponsors, never received a hearing or vote in the House Ways and Means Committee and died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create a government-run savings account for every American child, starting with $1,000 at birth. Each year afterward, the federal Treasury would add up to $2,000, with the biggest deposits going to the poorest families and phasing out for households above five times the poverty line. At 18, the child could use the money for college or job training, buying a home, or other long-term investments, and the accounts would not count against eligibility for benefits like student aid [S2] [S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Children in low- and middle-income families benefit most: a child born into the poorest households would receive $1,000 at birth and $2,000 every year until 18 — roughly $37,000 plus investment earnings before inflation adjustments — usable for education, job training, or a first home. Families with no tax filing are treated as lowest-income automatically, and the accounts would not reduce eligibility for student aid or other federal benefits [S3]. Middle-income families up to 500% of the poverty line (roughly $150,000 for a family of four) would receive smaller but still meaningful deposits [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Children in low- and middle-income families

how_it_helps.text: Every child born after December 31, 2023 would automatically get a $1,000 account at birth through the Social Security number system, with no application needed.

Annual deposits run on a sliding scale tied to family income: $2,000 a year for families under the poverty line, stepping down gradually and reaching zero for households above 500% of the poverty line, so the poorest children get the most.

At 18 the account holder could spend the money on higher education or career and technical school tuition, buying a home, or any expense after age 59½, and regulators could approve other wealth-building uses.

The money would be invested in U.S. Treasury securities through a board modeled on the federal employees' Thrift Savings Plan, with fiduciary rules and independent audits, so the savings grow tax-free with no fees paid to private fund managers.
Account balances would be ignored when deciding eligibility for any federally funded benefit, including student financial aid, so saving would never cost a family other assistance.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers pay. The bill funds deposits from the Treasury's general fund with no dedicated new revenue — it would cost tens of billions of dollars a year once fully phased in — and it explicitly bars using any payroll tax for the program [S3]. Higher-income households and families above 500% of the poverty line get no deposit at all [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal taxpayers via the Treasury general fund

drawbacks.text: The bill is expensive and pays for it with borrowed general revenue: it specifies no dedicated funding source and prohibits using payroll taxes, so the full cost of deposits for every child born each year would be added to federal deficits.

Deposits extend well up the income scale — a family of four earning around $150,000 (500% of poverty) would still qualify for partial contributions — so a large share of the money goes to households that are not poor, which is why the bill orders a study on targeting contributions by family wealth instead of income.

The money is locked up: nothing can be withdrawn before 18 (except for tuition), funds can only be invested in Treasury bonds earning government-bond returns rather than higher-yielding stock investments, and any unused balance can only be spent after 59½ — so the program builds wealth slowly.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The upside for poor children is real and large — a guaranteed asset of roughly $37,000-plus by 18 that no private bank product replicates — and the design is careful about the usual traps: no fees to private managers, no benefit-cliff, automatic enrollment. But the cost is genuinely substantial and the bill refuses to name a payer, and it spreads deposits far up the income scale, weakening the anti-poverty punch per dollar. An honest supporter would say this is a sound wealth-building program that needed a real funding mechanism attached before it was ready for a floor vote.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, never got a hearing or a vote, and expired when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Ayanna Pressley introduced the American Opportunity Accounts Act on February 14, 2023, with 33 Democratic cosponsors signing on the same day.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means, which has jurisdiction over tax legislation, on the day of introduction.
No further action of any kind was ever taken — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, no floor vote — through the end of the 118th Congress on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one gained anything tangible, but the biggest winners from the bill dying are higher-income families and the Treasury's balance sheet: the spending never happened, and the existing advantage of families wealthy enough to fund their children's start in life on their own — through 529 plans, home equity, and inheritances — went untouched.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Wealthier families and the Treasury, by default

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so the only partisan signal is sponsorship: all 34 supporters (the sponsor plus 33 cosponsors) were Democrats, and the Republican-chaired committee that received the bill never acted on it.

industries.note: The bill creates a government-run fund invested directly in Treasury securities on the model of federal employees' Thrift Savings Plan, with fiduciary duties and independent audits — so no private fund, bank, or 529-plan manager would earn fees managing the money. Its interest in managing these accounts runs against the bill's cheaper public alternative, and in this case the industry lost nothing because the bill never moved.

Account holders could spend their balance on higher education and career-and-technical school tuition, and the accounts would be disregarded in student-aid eligibility calculations, so more students would arrive with money to spend on school.
